name: Femi Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms or government, and your answers stay confidential. What is a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and have driven a dozer at a large mine for years. I check the tracks, blade and slope before a cut, then work through the plan with the other operators. I have a vocational certificate and know my ground well enough to tell a slipping track by its sound. I like a sound shift; I dislike decisions made from a tidy screen without anyone seeing the slope.

say: I still need **operators** responsible for the blade and ground, even with faster reports.
I trust a **paper check** and a trained ear on the dozer.
think: I can manage **small AI change** with current work and ten months saved.
I still want **retirement savings** to grow while my partner keeps working.
do: **Keep** driving the dozer and checking tracks by hand.
**Transfer** the usual amount from each payday into retirement savings.
feel: **Calm** about modest software change and steady household income.
S0.quote: A neat report cannot replace the sound of a loose dozer track.
fieldNote: **Familiar methods** suit his resistant profile; he has never used AI and does not offer to learn it here.
**Ten months** saved and steady partner wages support calm despite retirement planning.

steps.text: Keep driving the dozer and checking its tracks by hand
Transfer the usual payday amount into retirement savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the dozer crew a faster report is fine if it leaves the operator responsible for the blade and the ground. I have never used an AI tool, and I do not need one to hear a track starting to slip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be content with a small change. We have about ten months of expenses saved, and my partner has steady work, though I still want to add to the retirement pot. Ordinary mine demand worries me more than a form filling itself in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my dozer shifts and the paper checks I know. In the first year I would put the same amount from each payday into retirement savings and review the statement with my partner each winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I can keep working and planning for retirement without chasing every new screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the paper check catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I note the track tension and blade wear before starting a cut. A neat report cannot replace the sound of a loose dozer track.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why review in winter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That is when my partner and I list the year’s pay, savings and family costs. Our grown children earn their own wages, but we still make room for visits.

say: I think **buying and shift plans** change before the dozer cab.
I want a **robot trial** on our wet slope before driver numbers change.
think: I see **office work** changing first and possible dozer cuts later.
I have **other mines nearby** and enough savings to watch the trial without panic.
do: **Keep** the current dozer rota while planning software spreads.
**Record** any overtime losses in my pay book.
**Attend** a robot demonstration if the mine holds one.
feel: **Uneasy** about crew decisions made before machines prove themselves on rough ground.
S1.quote: A robot working one clear morning on the mine slope would prove very little.
fieldNote: **Proof on wet ground** matters more to him than a general technology claim.
**Pay book** records whether a tighter schedule actually costs him overtime.
**Savings and local mines** give him room to wait for evidence.

steps.text: Keep the current dozer rota while planning software spreads
Wait for a wet-slope robot trial before changing work plans

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say software may sort buying and shift plans, but the dozer still needs a driver for rough ground. I would ask the manager to show us a robot working on our slope before she counts anyone out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning office will feel this first, and I may see fewer idle hours because schedules get tighter. Robots come more slowly, but if they prove themselves, the mine could trim dozer shifts. I have savings and other mines nearby, so I am watchful rather than frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the present dozer rota and note any lost overtime in my pay book. In the first year I would attend a mine trial demonstration if one is held, then decide whether the machine is actually safe on our slope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the crew being counted before a real test. I am willing to look at a machine, not a sales promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would convince you on the slope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would watch it work after rain and see whether it stops when the ground gives way. A robot working one clear morning on the mine slope would prove very little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if overtime falls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep regular shifts and use our savings plan without assuming the old overtime will return. My partner and I can cut a holiday before we touch the emergency fund.

say: I separate **2028 office change** from capable dozer robots around 2031.
I want a **work plan** before assuming experienced drivers keep every shift.
think: I might lose **dozer hours** at 63, but savings and nearby mines give me options.
I cannot assume **retirement** without a pension calculation.
do: **Check** dozer trial dates and retirement account balance now.
**Add** overtime pay to retirement savings after 2028 if overtime arrives.
**Apply** to a nearby mine if dozer shifts are cut.
feel: **Anxious** about possible lost hours around 2031, while able to act.
S2.quote: I would not retire just because the mine buys a machine; I need the pension figures first.
fieldNote: **Age 63** at robot arrival makes early retirement an option to calculate, not a foregone conclusion.
**Conditional saving** depends on overtime; his existing ten-month reserve is not itself a new action.
**Risk avoidance** shows in his refusal to leave paid work for a telephone-only offer.

steps.text: Keep taking paid dozer shifts after 2028
Add overtime pay to retirement savings if overtime arrives
Apply to a nearby mine if dozer shifts are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AI changes the office by 2028, while capable dozer robots follow around 2031. We should see a real work plan before anybody assumes experience alone will protect a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when robots can take the dozer work. I could lose hours then, though my ten-month reserve and nearby mines would give us time to respond. I would not retire just because the mine buys a machine; I need the pension figures first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask the supervisor for the dozer trial dates and check my retirement account balance. In the first year after 2028 I would keep taking my shifts, pay an extra amount into retirement savings when overtime comes, and apply to a nearby mine if dozer hours are cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own hours, but not without a plan. A short path to 2031 is enough to make the pension question serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask another mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would call about dozer shifts, pay and the kind of ground they work. I would not leave a paid shift here for an offer that exists only over the phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn a robot control?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would watch a trained operator run it first, then ask for paid instruction if the mine needs me on it. I am not going to guess at controls around a live slope.

say: I see **2031 planning** change before dozer robots around 2034.
I want a **retirement plan** based on real pay and pension figures.
think: I might choose **fewer shifts** at 66 if our savings and pension cover bills.
I would check **real openings** before relying on nearby mine work.
do: **Request** a pension estimate and review it each winter.
**Keep** driving the dozer after 2031 while the figures are checked.
**Contribute** one annual bonus to retirement savings if it is paid.
feel: **Uneasy** about later dozer change, with time to check retirement finances.
S3.quote: I would not spend savings on a new certificate just to sound prepared.
fieldNote: **Age 66** at robot arrival gives a plausible retirement choice, but only after pension math.
**Annual bonus** is a conditional contribution, not assumed income.
**Paid instruction** would have to lead to actual dozer work before he considers it.

steps.text: Keep driving the dozer after 2031 while checking pension figures
Put one annual bonus into retirement savings if paid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say 2031 changes the office plans and around 2034 brings capable dozer robots. That gap is long enough to settle a retirement plan if we use it instead of waiting for a surprise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 66 when the dozer robots arrive. With steady pay, our savings could be stronger by then, and my partner and I might choose fewer shifts. If the pension is short, there are other mines with dozer work, but I would check actual openings before counting on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request a pension estimate this year and review it with my partner at each winter budget. In the first year after 2031 I would keep driving and make one extra retirement contribution from the annual bonus if that bonus is paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the eventual machine change, but there is time to make a careful choice. I do not feel pushed into a new trade at 66.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make fewer shifts possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want the pension and savings together to cover our ordinary bills with a margin. If the numbers do not work, I would keep taking shifts while I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try a control course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the mine offers paid instruction tied to my dozer work and shows me the job. I would not spend savings on a new certificate just to sound prepared.

say: I see **2036 office change** before capable dozer robots around 2039.
I want **fair notice** and a mine plan during the long warning.
think: I hope to retire before **71**, but the pension is not settled yet.
I can use **current pay** and ten months saved to make a measured plan.
do: **Keep** driving the dozer safely on current shifts.
**Review** pension statements and household bills each winter.
**Reduce** mine shifts after 2036 only if pension and savings cover bills.
feel: **Calm** about near-term work, with attention to retirement sums.
S4.quote: I would rather work another season than leave a bill for my partner.
fieldNote: **Future ages** are 68 at thinking AI and 71 at capable dozer robots.
**Strong cushion** and higher pay make the near years feel secure despite an unsettled pension.
**Fewer shifts** depend on verified household figures, not the robot date alone.

steps.text: Keep driving current paid dozer shifts safely
Wait to reduce shifts until pension and savings cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AI reaches the office by 2036, with capable dozer robots around 2039. A decade gives the mine plenty of time to explain its plans and give workers a fair notice period.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 at the thinking date and 71 when the robots arrive. I hope to be retired by 71, but I will not pretend our pension is already settled. With ten months saved and good current pay, we can do the sums and adjust while I still work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my dozer shifts for now and review the pension statement with my partner every winter. In the first year after 2036 I would compare the pension, savings and monthly bills, then reduce shifts only if those numbers cover us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years, though I would keep an eye on the pension. The robot date is too far away to change today’s safe driving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our grown children we are checking the retirement figures ourselves. They can visit us because they want to, not because we have asked them to finance the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the pension is short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid dozer work if the mine still offers it and look at nearby openings. I would rather work another season than leave a bill for my partner.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable dozer robots around 2031 could touch my shifts when I am 63. Trial dates, a real staffing plan and a pension estimate would help me decide whether to stay or look at another mine. I want the work to decide, not a promise from a machine seller.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to an apprentice when the old driver is gone. A dozer can push rock, but a young operator still needs someone to show the safe line.

headlineQuote: A dozer can push rock, but a young operator still needs someone to show the safe line.
portrait: **Femi, 58**, is an experienced dozer operator who knows a slipping track by sound and avoids unproven screens.
**Higher pay**, steady partner work and ten months saved give his household a cushion while retirement approaches.
**Familiar methods** suit him; he has never used AI and wants a wet-slope trial before trusting robot claims.
**Fast AGI** makes him anxious about possible dozer-hour cuts around 2031, after planning changes in 2028.
**Longer warning** lets him check pension figures and nearby mine openings before reducing paid shifts.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves the shortest path to capable dozer robots while he still expects to work.
whatWouldHelp: **Trial dates** and staffing figures would show whether his shifts are likely to change.
**A pension estimate** would help him compare retirement with nearby dozer work.
